trichophytic-closure.summary: A suturing method after strip harvesting that lets hair grow through the donor scar, so short haircuts look cleaner.

quick.overview:
Trichophytic closure is a way of closing the strip-harvest donor wound in a hair transplant (and facelift incisions) so hair grows through the scar and hides it. The payoff is a cleaner-looking back and sides, especially with a short haircut.

The wound edges are trimmed or stepped so follicles survive at the margin, and hair then grows through the healing scar. Published comparisons are small and mostly retrospective, such as a 2018 cohort of 46 facelift patients comparing W-plasty and straight-line closure on hairline scars.
quick.how: It is done by the surgeon at the time the donor strip is taken during a hair transplant, as part of how the wound is sutured. Patients see how the scar settles as the wound heals and hair grows through it over the following months. Variants such as double or asymmetric suture patterns are described for donor wounds.
quick.risks: It is a surgical closure with the usual wound risks, and scars can still be visible in some cases. It applies to strip (FUT) harvesting scars, not to follicle-by-follicle extraction.

angle.text: Hair transplant patients and surgeons use trichophytic closure after strip harvesting so hair grows through the donor scar, making a short haircut look cleaner. The camouflage is seen in the healed scar itself, and the supporting comparisons are small studies.

platelet-rich-fibrin-for-hair.summary: A fibrin clot made from your own blood, used in dental surgery and tried off-label by some clinics to thicken thinning hair.

quick.overview:
Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is made by spinning your own blood to form a platelet- and white-cell-rich fibrin clot, a relative of PRP. People try it on the scalp hoping for thicker-looking hair.

The platelets in the clot release growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF, and the fibrin acts as a scaffold near follicles. PRF is documented mainly in dental and oral surgery; for hair, one small registered trial of 10 participants compares it with PRP in female pattern hair loss, with no results published.
quick.how: It is an in-clinic procedure: blood is drawn, spun into a clot, and the material is placed in the scalp, much like PRP sessions. It is offered as an off-label aesthetic treatment, usually as a series of visits.
quick.risks: It is an injection-based procedure using your own blood. Risks specific to hair use are not described in published sources, and it is off-label for hair.

angle.text: Users and clinics try PRF on thinning scalp hair as a relative of PRP, hoping growth factors released near the follicles will thicken hair. It is documented mainly in dentistry, and one small registered trial has looked at hair.

hair-micropigmentation.summary: A scalp tattoo that gives the look of a buzz cut, adds apparent density to thin hair, or hides scars, with an immediate result.

quick.overview:
Scalp micropigmentation (SMP) tattoos tiny dots onto the scalp so it looks like closely shaved hair. People use it to look like they have a buzz cut on a bald scalp, to make a thin crown look denser, or to camouflage hair-transplant and other scars.

Pigment is placed in the superficial skin and matched to the client's existing hair colour, imitating the shadow of cropped hair. The result is visible right away and is described mainly in news and magazine coverage rather than peer-reviewed studies.
quick.how: It typically takes about three to four sessions of around two hours each. The look is long lasting, and touch-ups are used over time. It is usually worn with a closely cropped or shaved head.
quick.risks: Allergic reaction to the ink is a stated concern, and a poorly placed hairline can look unnatural. Removal requires laser. No peer-reviewed studies were identified.

angle.text: Men with hair loss get scalp micropigmentation to create the look of a buzz cut, add apparent density to a thin crown, or hide transplant scars. The pigment is visible immediately, and hairline placement determines how natural it looks.

eyelash-implants.summary: Surgical placement of hair into the eyelid margin to build longer, denser lashes, distinct from extensions and false lashes.

quick.overview:
Eyelash implants, also called eyelash transplantation, place hair into the eyelid margin so it grows as lashes. The goal is permanently fuller, more defined eyes without glued-on extensions.

Hair is set into the lid edge so it grows there as lashes. The sources reviewed describe the history of the idea, such as an 1882 report of hair sewn into the eyelids and an 1899 newspaper account, and contain no modern outcome studies.
quick.how: It is a surgical procedure done on the eyelid, unlike extensions or false lashes that are applied to or alongside existing lashes. People weighing it compare it with those removable options.
quick.risks: It is surgery on the eyelid, and historical accounts describe the early method as painful. No modern safety or outcome studies were found.

angle.text: People seeking permanently fuller lashes consider eyelash transplantation, which places hair into the eyelid margin so it grows as lashes. It differs from extensions and false lashes, and the sources reviewed give history only.

artificial-hair-integrations.summary: Extensions, weaves, hairpieces and mesh systems that add length and cover thinning areas immediately, and can be removed.

quick.overview:
Artificial hair integrations blend human or synthetic hair into your own to add length, volume and coverage, and to camouflage hair loss from conditions such as alopecia. The fuller look is there as soon as they are applied.

Added hair is clipped, bonded, sewn, fused or pulled through a mesh base so it merges with existing hair. Attachment methods include tape-in, clip-in, micro rings, fusion, weaving and wigs.
quick.how: They are non-surgical and reversible, used for styling and for hair-loss coverage. Synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon costs much less than human hair but wears out faster under heat and friction. No clinical trials were found.
quick.risks: Prolonged tension, such as tight braiding, can cause traction alopecia, and adhesives are linked to skin reactions, dermatitis and headaches.

angle.text: Users with thinning hair or alopecia use weaves, hairpieces and integration systems to add length, volume and coverage right away. Added hair is attached to their own so thin areas are covered; traction and adhesive issues are documented separately.

scalp-cooling-cap.summary: A cap that chills the scalp during chemotherapy to help you keep more of your hair, studied mainly in breast cancer patients.

quick.overview:
A scalp cooling cap lowers scalp temperature during chemotherapy so more of your hair is kept through treatment. It comes as frozen gel caps or machine-cooled systems.

Cooling is thought to reduce blood flow and drug exposure at the follicle and slow follicle activity while chemotherapy circulates. It has been evaluated mostly in women with breast cancer, including a randomized trial and cohort study published in JAMA in 2017, plus registries and systematic reviews.
quick.how: Gel or ice caps are frozen beforehand and swapped during the infusion, while machine systems keep coolant circulating through the cap from a control unit. It is used around chemotherapy sessions, particularly with taxane or anthracycline regimens. It preserves existing hair rather than growing new hair.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally minor. Caps are not advised where cancer is in the scalp skin or in lymphoma or leukemia, and a meta-analysis has examined scalp metastasis risk. US costs are roughly $1,500 to $3,000 per course.

angle.text: Chemotherapy patients wear scalp cooling caps to keep more of their hair through treatment: the chilled scalp reduces how much drug reaches the follicles. It has been studied in trials, mainly in breast cancer patients, and preserves existing hair rather than boosting growth.

intralesional-corticosteroid-scalp-injec.summary: Clinic-given steroid injections into patchy hair-loss spots, mainly alopecia areata and eyebrows, to bring hair back in those areas.

quick.overview:
Small amounts of corticosteroid, commonly triamcinolone, are injected into patches of alopecia areata or areas of eyebrow loss to restore hair in those spots.

The steroid acts locally to calm the immune attack on hair follicles. A 2020 systematic review reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of patients at one concentration, while up to 80 percent of people with one or two small patches regrow within a year without treatment.
quick.how: It is a clinic-administered prescription treatment, used where hair loss patches on the head are small or where eyebrow hair has been lost. Several registered trials are comparing it with other treatments.
quick.risks: It is a prescription procedure for alopecia areata. The sources reviewed do not detail side effects of the injections, and spontaneous regrowth in small patches makes results harder to interpret.

angle.text: Dermatologists inject triamcinolone into small patches of alopecia areata, including eyebrow loss, to restore hair in those spots by calming the local immune attack on follicles. A 2020 review reported high regrowth rates, though many small patches regrow on their own.

in-office-laser-whitening.summary: A dentist applies peroxide gel and aims a light or laser at the teeth for a visibly brighter smile in one visit.

quick.overview:
In-office laser whitening is a dentist-delivered bleaching treatment where a strong peroxide gel is applied and a light or laser unit is aimed at the teeth. People book it to get a brighter smile in a single visit.

The peroxide breaks down stain molecules inside the tooth, and the light is marketed as speeding that up. Wikipedia reports typical changes of 2 to 7 shades lasting months, with some rebound in the first week; reviews have examined whether the light adds anything beyond the gel alone.
quick.how: It is done in the dental chair, with the gums covered by a barrier, in one session. Results last months, and some colour can return in the first week.
quick.risks: Tooth sensitivity is the most commonly reported side effect, lasting days to weeks in some studies. Unprotected gums can be burned by strong gels, and heat from the light is a reported concern.

angle.text: People wanting a brighter smile in one visit choose in-office whitening with a light or laser unit. A dentist applies peroxide gel and the teeth shift several shades lighter on the spot; reviews are still comparing results with and without the light.

zoom-whitening.summary: A branded dentist-applied peroxide-and-lamp whitening session that lightens teeth several shades in one visit.

quick.overview:
Zoom whitening is a well-known in-office treatment in which dental staff apply a strong peroxide gel and expose it to a lamp. People book it for a quick, visibly whiter smile, often before events or other cosmetic work.

The gel releases oxidising agents that lighten stain inside enamel and dentin, and the lamp is intended to speed the process. In-office power bleaching generally uses roughly 25-38% hydrogen peroxide with 6-15 minutes of light exposure, and Wikipedia reports changes of 2 to 7 shades lasting months.
quick.how: It is a single dentist-chair session, with the gums protected by a barrier. Research mostly addresses in-office bleaching in general rather than this brand.
quick.risks: Sensitivity is common and usually temporary. Gums are protected with a barrier because strong peroxide can burn tissue.

angle.text: Zoom is a branded dentist-applied whitening session people book for a quick, visibly whiter smile, typically before events or other cosmetic work. Shade improvement is routinely recorded, as in other in-office power bleaching.

gum-depigmentation.summary: Dentist-performed lightening of dark, melanin-pigmented gums by scalpel, laser or chemicals for a more even pink gumline.

quick.overview:
Gum depigmentation lightens gums that are dark because of melanin, whether from genetics or smoking, for a pinker, more even gumline and a brighter-looking smile.

Pigmented surface tissue is removed or ablated by scalpel, laser or chemical agents, and the gum heals with new, lighter tissue. Published trials are mostly small and compare techniques such as scalpel surgery, diode and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers, microsurgery, bur-based methods and microneedling.
quick.how: It is a cosmetic periodontal procedure done by a dentist, with the colour change visible after healing. Technique choice affects recovery, and laser-treated gums heal by secondary intention.
quick.risks: Recovery is longer after scalpel surgery, and chemical methods can have side effects. Pigment recurrence is reported inconsistently.

angle.text: People with dark, melanin-pigmented gums have them lightened by scalpel, laser or chemical methods for a more even pink gumline. The new lighter tissue shows once the gums heal, and the studies so far are small technique comparisons.

enameloplasty-tooth-reshaping.summary: A dentist smooths or shaves tiny amounts of enamel to fix chips, uneven edges or tooth length, with an immediate result.

quick.overview:
Enameloplasty, also called tooth reshaping or contouring, removes a little enamel to change how a tooth looks, such as shortening a pointed edge, smoothing a chip or evening out an edge. The result is immediate.

A dentist uses fine instruments to remove and smooth enamel, changing the tooth's contours. Wikipedia describes it as giving fast results and sometimes standing in for braces; no clinical studies on the cosmetic use were found.
quick.how: It is a quick chairside procedure, often used for small tweaks, sometimes instead of braces. The same term is also used in dentistry for widening fissures before sealants and adjusting bite surfaces.
quick.risks: Removed enamel does not grow back, and dentin may be exposed.

angle.text: Users get tooth reshaping to smooth chips, even out edges or tweak tooth length quickly, sometimes in place of braces. A dentist removes small amounts of enamel and the change shows immediately.

porcelain-veneers.summary: Thin custom ceramic shells bonded to the front of teeth to change colour, shape and spacing in one makeover, lasting 10 to 30 years.

quick.overview:
Porcelain veneers are custom ceramic shells bonded to front teeth to change their colour, shape, size or gaps, giving a brighter, uniform smile. They are a staple of smile-focused makeovers.

A dentist usually removes some enamel and takes an impression or scan; a lab makes the shells, which are etched and bonded with resin cement. They are among the more studied cosmetic restorations, including a 2016 meta-analysis and a ten-year trial following 87 veneers in 25 patients, and Wikipedia gives lifespans of 10 to 30 years.
quick.how: Treatment takes multiple visits: preparation, impressions or scans, then bonding of the lab-made shells. Wax-ups or mock-ups are often used beforehand to preview the result. Veneers are replaced when they chip, debond, discolour or decay.
quick.risks: Reported risks are sensitivity, decay, debonding and fracture. Preparation can remove a meaningful part of the tooth surface and is generally permanent, critics argue veneers are overused, and costs are substantial.

angle.text: Veneers change tooth colour, shape, size or gaps in one makeover, and are a staple of smile-focused looksmaxxing. The result is plainly visible, and follow-up studies report long-lasting restorations.

maryland-bridge.summary: A false tooth with wings glued behind neighbouring teeth, filling a gap with little drilling; debonding is the usual failure.

quick.overview:
A Maryland bridge replaces a missing tooth, often a front tooth, with a false tooth carrying metal or ceramic wings that are glued behind the adjacent teeth. The gap is visibly closed once it is placed.

The wings are bonded to acid-etched enamel on the back surface of neighbouring teeth, holding the replacement tooth in the gap. It needs little or no preparation, so it preserves more natural tooth than a conventional bridge.
quick.how: It is used as a conservative way to fill a gap, especially at the front. Designs with a single wing on one side (cantilever) are reported to have fewer complications than designs bonded on both sides.
quick.risks: Debonding is the main concern and can let decay start under a loose wing. It is not suited to people who grind their teeth, have mobile teeth or have a nickel allergy.

angle.text: People missing a tooth use a Maryland bridge to fill the gap with little drilling of neighbouring teeth. The bonded wings hold a replacement tooth in place and the gap is closed once placed; debonding is the usual failure noted.

gum-graft.summary: Surgery that moves gum tissue over exposed roots to restore the gumline; mainly for recession, sometimes sought for looks.

quick.overview:
A gum graft covers exposed tooth roots or thickens thin gum by moving tissue from the palate, from next to the tooth, or from a processed donor matrix. It is mainly a periodontal treatment for recession, and some people seek it because front teeth look long.

The tissue is placed over the exposed root and sutured so it heals in place. A 2018 literature review summarised on Wikipedia reported that recession was reduced after most root coverage procedures, and registered trials continue to compare techniques.
quick.how: It is usually performed by a periodontist. Variants differ in where the tissue comes from: the palate, adjacent gum, donor matrix or blood-derived fibrin. Not all recession requires surgery.
quick.risks: Pain is the most commonly reported effect, mainly at the palatal donor site. Pedicle grafts can cause donor-site recession, and donor matrices carry healing and disease-transmission considerations.

angle.text: Gum grafts are done mainly for recession, and some seek them to cover exposed roots and even out the gumline so front teeth look less long. The surgical result is visible once healed; the cosmetic use sits alongside the dental one.

gum-lift.summary: Reshaping the gumline, sometimes with bone, to show more tooth and soften a gummy smile.

quick.overview:
A gum lift reshapes the gumline to expose more of the tooth, rebalancing a gummy smile or short-looking teeth. It overlaps with crown lengthening, a procedure done by periodontists.

Gum tissue is removed and sometimes supporting bone is reshaped to a lower level, with the flap repositioned. Braces to extrude the tooth are an alternative. No registered trials directly study cosmetic gum lifts; sources describe the technique and its trade-offs.
quick.how: A periodontist performs it, with the change visible after healing. Soreness typically lasts one to two weeks. Cosmetic dentistry sources describe gum contouring as making teeth look longer or more even.
quick.risks: Bone removal is irreversible and can weaken neighbouring support and complicate implants. The gum margin may drift back toward the crown over time.

angle.text: Users with a gummy smile or short-looking teeth have the gumline reshaped to show more tooth, overlapping with crown lengthening. The change shows once the gums heal, and research specific to cosmetic use is limited.

internal-bleaching.summary: Whitening a darkened root-canal-treated tooth from the inside so it matches its neighbours; high immediate success is reported.

quick.overview:
Internal bleaching lightens a dark, root-canal-treated tooth, often at the front, so it matches the rest of the smile. The agent is sealed inside the tooth instead of applied to the outer surface.

Hydrogen peroxide, applied directly or produced from sodium perborate or carbamide peroxide, breaks down the pigment inside the tooth. A critical review reported over 90% immediate success, with 10 to 40% of treated teeth needing re-treatment within 1 to 8 years.
quick.how: The bleaching agent is replaced every few weeks over successive visits until the desired shade is reached. It is used for non-vital teeth, which lose their nerve supply and often darken.
quick.risks: Cervical root resorption is the main documented concern, linked especially to heated (thermocatalytic) methods. Dentine weakening and crown fracture have also been described.

angle.text: People with a single darkened root-canal-treated tooth, often at the front, use internal bleaching to match it to the rest of the smile. The bleach works from inside the tooth, and reports describe high immediate success with some re-treatment needed.

bite-reclamation.summary: Rebuilding worn-down teeth to restore bite height and a fuller lower face, as part of full-mouth reconstruction.

quick.overview:
Bite reclamation reopens a bite that has collapsed from tooth wear, such as from grinding or acid reflux, restoring the height of the lower face. Worn teeth can leave the lower face looking shortened, with the chin close to the nose.

Worn teeth are rebuilt so the jaws meet at a greater vertical dimension. It is described as part of complex full-mouth reconstruction involving many teeth; only brief encyclopedic descriptions were found, with no trials.
quick.how: It is large restorative dental work covering many teeth, usually planned and staged by a dentist. Temporaries or previews are often used to check appearance and bite.
quick.risks: Sources describe the work as complex, and no safety data specific to the procedure were found.

angle.text: Those with teeth worn down by grinding or acid use bite reclamation to rebuild height, which can make the lower face look less shortened. Teeth are restored so the jaws meet higher, as part of full-mouth reconstruction.

wax-up-smile-mock-up.summary: A model or temporary preview of planned tooth changes, used before veneers to check size, shape and smile line.

quick.overview:
A wax-up or mock-up previews planned cosmetic tooth changes so you and your dentist can judge size, shape and proportion before treatment, usually ahead of veneers.

A model or temporary is shaped to the planned result and tried against the lips and smile line, showing how changes relate to the gums, lips and smile. It can also test speech and bite. Digital smile design is a related software approach, with one registered crossover trial of 44 participants comparing AI-assisted and conventional versions.
quick.how: The dentist builds a model of the planned teeth, then temporaries based on it are worn to see appearance, speech and bite. It guides tooth preparation before final veneers are made.
quick.risks: The preview itself is non-permanent, and the sources describe no specific risks of the mock-up.

angle.text: Patients planning veneers use a wax-up or mock-up to see proposed tooth changes against their lips and smile before committing. The preview can be seen and tried in the mouth, then guides the final result.

surgical-orthodontics.summary: Jaw surgery coordinated with braces to correct bite and facial proportions; established medicine with a long recovery.

quick.overview:
Surgical orthodontics combines braces with corrective jaw surgery to fix bite problems, airway issues and facial imbalance, including receding chins, underbites, overbites and asymmetry. Appearance is among the stated goals, and the jaw position and profile change visibly.

Orthodontists align the teeth, and an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cuts and repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw or chin, usually through the mouth, fixing it with plates and screws. Studies report high post-surgical satisfaction, alongside depressive reactions during recovery in some patients.
quick.how: Treatment is coordinated between an orthodontist and a surgeon, and some patients have surgery before braces. Initial healing takes 2 to 6 weeks and bone union a further 2 to 4 months. The term is also used for surgically facilitated orthodontics, such as corticotomy, which aims to speed tooth movement.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months. It is major surgery with weeks to months of recovery.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers consider jaw surgery with braces to correct bite, airway and facial imbalance, including recessed or overlong jaws. The jaw bone is repositioned, so the change in jaw position and profile is visible afterward.

all-on-4.summary: A full arch of fixed teeth held by four implants, replacing failing teeth with a complete, uniform smile.

quick.overview:
All-on-4 replaces a whole arch of teeth with a fixed bridge held by four implants, two of them angled to avoid grafting. Teeth are usually fitted within about a day of surgery, giving a new, uniform smile. In looksmaxxing circles it is filed under hardmaxx dental work for people with failing or missing teeth.

Titanium implants fuse with the jaw bone, and the tilted rear implants use denser front bone and avoid sinus and nerve areas. Follow-up studies from the originating group report high implant survival over several years, though much early research was manufacturer-funded and independent trials are small.
quick.how: A bridge screwed onto the implants is worn full-time. It is aimed at tooth loss rather than facial change, and trials of framework materials and implant configurations are ongoing.
quick.risks: Reported issues include wear of acrylic teeth, bone loss around implants, infection and implant failure. Costs are high and vary widely by country.

angle.text: People with failing teeth choose All-on-4 to get a full fixed arch in a new, uniform smile, which looksmaxxing culture files under hardmaxx dental work. It is established dental surgery with high reported implant survival, aimed at tooth loss rather than facial change.
